title: Local-LLM fine-tuning stack ships CUDA/ROCm parity as the default by H2 2027
body: Unsloth, the library that squeezes large-model fine-tuning onto small GPUs, shipped official AMD support on July 20, built jointly with AMD's own engineering team, and it did so with the claim that matters most: the same headline numbers it posts on Nvidia — up to twice the speed and about 70% less VRAM at no accuracy loss — now hold on AMD Radeon, Ryzen AI and Instinct parts, from consumer RX 9000 cards to MI350 datacenter GPUs, across Windows, WSL and Linux. The detail underneath the release is where the bottleneck has actually been. AMD's silicon was not the gap; the tooling was, because the fine-tuning and local-inference stack grew up CUDA-first and ROCm support was a porting afterthought that broke often enough to send hobbyists and researchers back to Nvidia by reflex. What Unsloth proved this week is that closing that gap is fundable — that a vendor willing to put its own engineers on the port can reach genuine performance parity, not a slower it-runs fallback. The prediction is that this stops being one library's headline and becomes the cohort's default. By H2 2027, cross-vendor parity is the norm across the open local-LLM fine-tuning stack: at least two more major open fine-tuning toolkits beyond Unsloth — among Axolotl, TRL, Llama-Factory, torchtune and the PEFT front ends — ship official ROCm backends that document the same speed and memory numbers they claim on CUDA rather than a caveated best-effort mode, and day-zero support for a newly released open model lands on ROCm at the same time as CUDA rather than as a later, breakage-prone follow-on. The force behind the call is competitive and economic rather than technical. Once one stack demonstrates that ROCm parity ships and that a hardware vendor will co-fund the engineering to get it, the CUDA-first ordering every toolkit inherited becomes a liability rather than a safe default, and a chipmaker with a credible second-source position has every reason to bankroll the same work across the rest of the cohort. What would falsify the call is durable second-class status: if through H2 2027 ROCm stays an it-runs-but-slower backend that lands weeks behind CUDA across the major toolkits, with Unsloth the lone exception and no peer posting parity numbers, the prediction is wrong.

reasoning.because: Unsloth shipped AMD-co-engineered ROCm support matching its Nvidia speed and VRAM claims
reasoning.given: Fine-tuning tooling grew up CUDA-first, so ROCm was a break-prone afterthought, not a silicon gap
reasoning.so_that: Two-plus more open fine-tuning toolkits ship parity ROCm backends and new-model coverage lands on ROCm and CUDA at once
reasoning.landing: by H2 2027; 2+ peer toolkits document ROCm parity; day-zero coverage on both
reasoning.plain_language: AI-tuning tools used to work best on Nvidia chips. Now one runs just as fast on AMD, so soon most tools will too.

summary: Unsloth shipped official AMD-co-engineered ROCm support matching its Nvidia speed and VRAM numbers, proving cross-vendor fine-tuning parity is fundable. Expect two-plus major open fine-tuning toolkits to ship parity ROCm backends, with new-model coverage landing on both vendors at once, by H2 2027.
